articles.text: Senators Vest and Cockrell are blatant hypocrites. They are both opposing the admission of Dakota bitterly, and can advance no other reason for their opposition than that it will give two or four more republican senators if Dakota is admitted in whole or part to the union. They are now ranting against the lease of the Indian reservations to cattle men when it has been proven that their opposition comes solely from the fact that they wanted the land for some friends and could not get it. We would suggest to these two honorable gentlemen that Dakota is a splendid summer resort, and that if they should conclude to visit us they will be accorded a warm reception. We will also guarantee that they will make their stay permanent, as they will be "stuck" on the country so that they will never leave.
articles.summary: Editorial denouncing Senators Vest and Cockrell for opposing Dakota's admission and reservation leases to cattlemen.

articles.headline: Retribution.
articles.text:
The Pierre coach on which Mr. J. C. Ryan was a passenger, upset on Cheyenne hill Wednesday. Mr. Ryan sustained a severe injury in the shoulder, and was otherwise badly bruised up. Arriving home Christmas evening it was found that the cap of the left shoulder was fractured. While the injury is painful, Dr. Louthan pronounces it not necessarily very serious.—[Dakota Register.

The above points a moral and adorns the following tale: Mr. Ryan went east via Medora, and while here made rates for the shipment of a large lot of groceries. He, in company with every other business man of Spearfish, had agreed to ship every pound of their freight and express via Medora, conditioned upon the stages running through Spearfish. He was given the very lowest rates—and shipped via Belfield. In going east, Mr. Ryan claimed to have been too frequently smashed up on the other lines to try them again and, as he had signed the contract to ship via Medora, and had repeatedly promised to help the line in every way he could, it was considered a matter of course that he would both ship and travel our way. He could not, by any possibility, have received a rate five cents lower than the one offered here without loss to the forwarder. Notwithstanding the fact that the Medora line has at any and all times said that any opposition rate would be met, he learned the lowest straight rate and then accepted a lower rate without giving the company here a chance even to meet it. He either had other business or a pass via the Pierre route on his return and took that way. The Medora line does not go begging for business, but like other business institutions, believes in living up to its contracts. It then sees no reason why Mr. Ryan or any other man should not live up to the terms of the one he signed.
articles.summary: J. C. Ryan of Spearfish, injured when the Pierre coach upset, is chided for shipping via Belfield despite a contract with the Medora line.

articles.headline: A Communication.
articles.text:
BISMARCK, Dak., Dec. 31, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY—Dear Sir:—Will you kindly allow a few facts in your valuable paper, regarding the vast amount of good and general benefit that the Marquis de Mores (N. P. R. C. Co.) has done for the general public, the working people especially. Heretofore prices of meat were very high in this section of the country, and are still at the retail markets, simply because a few retail dealers in each town combined to make them so. In the opinion of many thinking men, beef should be as cheap here as in Chicago, if not cheaper, whereas cattle are raised in thousands and shipped in hundreds of cars to eastern markets, paying high freightage, etc., and slaughtered and sold there cheaper than people here at home could buy. Now that the N. P. R. C. Co. has established storage and sale rooms in many prominent towns and accommodate the people with low prices, the enmity of the retail dealers is roused against them, and they will not buy of them except where necessity compels it.

The consumers in many districts should in my opinion, request of the company to establish retail markets and give the company all their patronage, and show these few combined dealers that they must keep pace with the progression of civilization and come to the standard of the times. The people here should cherish warm feelings toward the said company from the fact that they have spent, and are spending, thousands upon thousands of dollars here helping to build up the country, and filling one of the greatest necessities of the country.

Let thinking people stop and consider the number of men that this company gives employment to, not only in the summer season, but in the dull winter, filling their ice houses and getting prepared for the spring trade. The company will, at some near future day, reap the benefits of its good work by a liberal patronage of the people.

OBSERVER.
articles.summary: Letter from 'Observer' in Bismarck praising the Marquis de Mores' N. P. R. C. Co. for lowering meat prices.

articles.text: The famous Staked Plains of Texas, as everybody who has looked at the maps of the country knows, are in the northern part of the State and lap over into New Mexico. Since they were first staked, nearly fifty years ago, they have been considered as mostly worthless; with plenty of grass but nary drop to drink. But of late wells affording splendid water are being dug, and the welcome fluid springs up at any time after twenty feet has been reached. This water not only supplies stock, but enough is expected to be obtained to use successfully for irrigating purposes.—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipped item on wells on the Staked Plains of Texas.

articles.text: The reports from the cattle region all along the Northern Pacific and through Montana, are to the effect that the weather out there in all respects is just as good as could be asked for by the cattle men, and the cattle are all in excellent condition. In Colorado, all through those ranges of mountains there is great cause for complaint. That country has been heavily visited with snow and the cattle are suffering very seriously in consequence. A letter received in St. Paul yesterday from a gentleman who has been out all through Colorado says that it has been very cold in western Kansas and eastern Colorado, and that stock has suffered very seriously indeed in consequence. It seems that the territory of Montana is proving to be the best country in the world to raise cattle in. It does not seem to be so seriously afflicted with snow as are the territories that are further south. The Montana and Bad Lands cattle stand very high in the eastern markets, and seem to be quite able to maintain the position they now occupy.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Clipped report that cattle along the Northern Pacific and in Montana are in excellent condition while Colorado suffers.

articles.text: Assistant Secretary of the Interior Joslyn is "away up" on Indians, and the estimation in which their abilities are held by cattle men. He advances as a reason for leasing the reservations that the "Indians being employed as herders learn how to care for and raise cattle." We have had some cold weather lately, but it was tropical in comparison to the day in which stockmen will employ Indians as herders.
articles.summary: Editorial jab at Assistant Secretary Joslyn's claim that Indians would learn herding on leased reservations.

articles.text: There are many brood mares in the country whose owners are so careless in regard to the kind of horses they raise that the true value of them is not known. Were such animals in proper hands they would soon make their mark as breeders. The man who is judge enough to select such mares as would produce a good colt each year could find but few better ways to invest his money, should he handle them properly and breed them with judgment.—[Stock Growers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on brood mares.

articles.text: Farmer Hartzell, of the South Park, who raises from two to three hundred high-grade calves each year, takes the youngsters from the cows as early as December, and after keeping them in a close corral until they are gentle and become accustomed to the presence of men, turns them into a field and feeds them hay until spring. "This," says he, "puts my yearlings six months ahead of my neighbors, and at two years of age they are equal to ordinary three-year-olds."—[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Farmer Hartzell's calf-feeding methods.

articles.text: Mr. T. W. Longley, manager of the Green Mountain Stock Ranching company, whose range is on Emmels creek, made the Stock Growers' a call New Year's morning. He says all the old range cattle are doing better than was expected, none of them dying, and not drifting to any extent, as feed is good and abundant. The through cattle that were poor in the fall are not doing so well. North of the Yellowstone cattle are drifting badly, and line riders are kept busy driving them back from the river. A few are crossing at the mouth of Rosebud. His company are wintering some stallions up Pumpkin creek, and Mr. Longley is on his way to this ranch. He says they have some native range stallions running with their cattle which are as fat as they can roll and don't seem to mind the cold weather.—[Stock Growers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped report from T. W. Longley of the Green Mountain Stock Ranching company on range conditions.

articles.text: At a recent dinner of a farmers' club in England, some speeches were made which are of interest to the American cattle men. Mr. Marston Frewen, of Wyoming, said that there were immense herds of cattle in that territory perfectly healthy and free from epidemic, and that pleuro pneumonia was absolutely unknown there. The far west could supply England with dairy cows at $60 a head, and grazing beasts at low prices, with which it would be profitable to stock their present unoccupied lands. That the present low prices were due to low freight charges, and the English farmers would be very foolish to neglect the present opportunity to replenish their declining agriculture. If the farmers of Great Britain adopt this advice it will open another market for ranchmen of this continent.—[St. Paul Globe.
articles.summary: Clipped report of Marston Frewen's speech in England on American cattle.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper was interviewed by a Pioneer Press reporter recently and we can't help but belive that either the reporter on the types misquoted him. He is credited with saying that 50 por cent. of the pilgrim cattle will succumb to the recent cold snap. It may have been that he said 5 per cent. or even 10 per cent. but either estimate is too high. We have recently spoken with nearly every stockmen on the Little Missouri, especially these who shipped in pilgrims last fall and the highest estimate is 3 per cent. Down the river there seems no doubt that the loss will be scarcely 2 per cent. Up the river there are several bunches of states yearlings that were driven in late and the loss may be as high as 3 per cent., certainly not higher. The interview alluded to has caused much comment and we have received many telegrams and letters relative to it. To all we have answered substantially as above. The old cattle, or these who have passed a winter here, are doing as well as the most sanguine could wish. The loss among this class is almost nothing. From the most authentic sources we think we are about the figure in quoting the per cent. of loss on all the Bad Lands cattle at one and a half per cent.
articles.summary: Editorial disputes C. W. Sleeper's reported 50 per cent loss estimate; Little Missouri losses put at about 1.5 to 3 per cent.

articles.text: The Northwestern Live Stock Journal lets its vials of wrath descend upon our devoted head in a way calculated to make it ache. It states that we quoted an article from the Journal without credit, attempted to give it some advice and then make a mistake in our figures. The above is all right with the exception that we never republished an article without credit and consider that an editor who will do so is as low as any other thief; that we have never under any circumstances ever made a comment on such an article republished from the Journal, as we considered it good authority on all stock matters; and finally could have made no mistake in figures if we made no comment on them. The Journal is a little too soon. It can be sure that when we attempt to disprove any of its assertions we will be well fortified with figures. We would also like to have the Journal editor look over our files and we will allow its "bad man" to take a shot at us for every clipping that we have published without credit. We have too many times expressed our opinion of editors whose paucity of brains compels them to write original editorials with their shears to be caught napping.
articles.summary: Editorial reply to the Northwestern Live Stock Journal's charge that the Cow Boy reprinted it without credit.

articles.text: The weather report in this issue, compiled by Mr. Martin, will attract attention as containing the coldest day ever experienced in this country. All over the states the 31st of December will be membered as a day in which old Boreas got in his work to the tune of thirty-five to fifty degrees below.
articles.summary: Note on Martin's weather report and the record cold of December 31.

articles.text: The first through train from the west on the Northern Pacific will come through in the morning. There has been the largest blockade of snow on record between Portland and the Dalles. Trains from the east have generally been on time, but those from the west, made up at Wallula, were from two to eighteen hours late.
articles.summary: First through N. P. train from the west expected after a snow blockade.

articles.text: A mournful state of affairs disclosed itself as the snow gradually yielded to the warmth of the chinook last Saturday. For several hours the life-size sign on our roof conveyed to the populace the information that there dwelt herein or that the sign had something to do with a "Bad —— —— Boy." It wasn't long, however, before the rest of the snow went, and the whole sign burst forth in effulgent splendor.
articles.summary: The chinook melted snow off the Cow Boy's roof sign.

articles.text: There has been considerable discussion relative to the abolishing of the herd law in West Missouri papers, and there is much less opposition to it than was expected. This year's experience has clearly shown the farmers that success lies in diversified farming and not in the exclusive culture of oats and wheat. Hence more stock must be raised, and then will come the necessity of a fence law.
articles.summary: Herd law discussion in West Missouri papers.

articles.text: Harry Gregg, of Spearfish, formerly superintendent of the Homestake mine, and now member of the legislature for Lawrence county, came in on the coach yesterday, and this morning left for Bismarck. He was "held up" by the COW BOY, and we are happy to state that he will be one of the strongest workers for the repeal of the herd law here, or at least the adoption of a fence law. Mr. Gregg is both a ranchman and a stockman in the Hills, and says that in Lawrence county, where the fence law prevails, there is no difficulty whatever between the ranchers and cattlemen. Mr. Gregg will be one of the most influential men in the legislature, and we can look forward to some good work being done for the relief of our stockmen. Mr. Gregg also appreciates the folly of chopping up our counties into little blocks to perpetuate the names of a defunct legislature, and will also labor to extend the county lines.
articles.summary: Legislator Harry Gregg of Spearfish passed through and pledged to work for herd-law repeal or a fence law.
